Would the minister explain the increase in this vote?

There are two items
of increase:	Permanent salaries, $13,876, and
temporary salaries, $18,362, making an increase on account of salaries of $32,238.
How many greenhouses at the central experimental farm are used for disease surveys and research work?

There are two in
cereals, two in botany, one in horticulture and one in forage crops.
Are there many people employed at the experimental farm who are not on the experimental staff but are classified as temporary employees, and have been there for a considerable number of years?

I have not the exact
figure, but there are very few who have been temporary over a considerable number of years.

I was informed that quite
a number of exceptionally well qualified men are on what is called the temporary staff. They are doing good work and have been there. I will not say a considerable number of years, but quite a number of years, and I was wondering what the chances were of their being made permanent in order to get the benefits of that classification.

Most of them were
student labourers who were taken on at the end of their courses. They are now reclassified under the reorganization, and will have a better opportunity of becoming permanent under the new set-up.

Driving along Carling
avenue I noticed an immense building being erected on the experimental farm. I should like to know why that building was erected, what was the necessity for it and what department it is for.
It is being erected by the Department of Public Works for the storing of records of the different departments. It has nothing to do with the operation of the experimental farm.

I notice that there
is an increase in this and the next item totalling $121,000. It is my opinion that there is a tremendous overhead in operating the experimental farm and the branch farms and stations.

That might perhaps
be better discussed under the next item. The one before us deals with the central experimental farm only.

The seasonal labourers
at the central experimental farm, who are mostly farmers' sons, receive from twenty-eight to thirty-four cents an hour, while the labourers employed by and under the Public Works department receive forty-five cents an hour. What is the reason for the difference in pay?

The main explanation is that the labour employed on the farm is agricultural labour. On our farms generally across the country we try to regulate the pay so that it will be somewhat in conformity with the general rate of pay prevailing for that type of labour. The Public Works department have what under their classification are called labourers but they are of a little different type from those we employ for general field work on the farm. There is also in connection with the Public Works classification some provision with which I am not fully familiar which has to do with the granting of holidays, and which works in with the rate of pay.

The seasonal worker at the farm, that is the farmer's son, has to work in the summer time fifty-eight hours a week, and in the winter fifty-three hours, whereas those employed under the Public Works department work only forty-four hours a week, or an eight-hour day. I should like to know why this distinction is made between these classes of labour.

The reason for it, I suppose, is largely one of custom and practice. In connection with artisans, for example, there is an eight-hour day, and speaking generally we adhere to that as a government. But there are no set hours for agricultural labour, and I think most of us realize that it would be difficult to operate a farm on an eight-hour basis. The farm is operated on a ten-hour basis.
Item agreed to.

Supply-Agriculture-Branch Farms
Branch farms and stations and illustration stations, $1,365,692.
How many of these stations are now in operation?
There are 26 experimental farms and stations, and in addition we have 9 substations and 194 illustration stations.
Does the farm of Doctor Saeger Wheeler that was taken over at Rosthern come in this list?
No. My information is that that farm is not included in the figures I have just given.
Under what branch of the department is it operated? I thought it was taken over as a substation.

Mr. Wheeler, of course, was a very prominent worker in the selection of seed and in the showing of wheat at exhibitions. He cooperated with the department until he reached the age of superannuation, and then he went off automatically. The question whether he should be further continued is still under consideration.

I have had letters from several persons in that district, also resolutions passed, I think, by the Prince Albert board of trade, asking me to make representations that Doctor Wheeler be continued in the service. I understand that when his farm was taken over as a demonstration farm he was employed as a superintendent at a salary, I think, of $2,200, until he reached the age of seventy. He reached that age last year, I understand, and I am informed by the Prince Albert board of trade that he was superannuated or given a pension of seven-fiftieths of his salary. They think that Doctor Wheeler is quite capable of still carrying on this work; he is very active, and has certainly made an important contribution to agriculture in the development of pure seed, as the minister has just stated. I have been asked to make representations on his behalf that he be allowed to carry on that work at the farm for another few years. He was one of the pioneer settlers; he has certainly made a valuable contribution to agriculture, and I am very glad to make these representations on his behalf. A statement from the minister as to the work Doctor Wheeler is actually carrying on, and whether the suggestion will be considered, would I think be very welcome at this time.

The department have not had the farm of Seager Wheeler rented. He has been carrying on experiments on his own farm, which I believe is located just across 
the road from our experimental branch there, and I think for seven years he has been paid a salary by the department to carry on his activities on his own farm and be available at all times for advisory purposes to our station across the road. Until he reached the age of seventy that pay was continued. When he reached the age of seventy the matter of superannuation was considered. The general policy is not to continue men beyond the age of seventy, but representations have been made by the board of trade of Prince Albert and others that we should reconsider the matter. We have it under consideration at the moment, but no further decision has been reached. At present he is superannuated.
I notice that there are three branch laboratories in the prairie provinces which are concerned largely with the diseases of cereals. Where are the three located?
That comes under the next item, science services. They are at Winnipeg, Saskatoon and Edmonton.

There is a sub-experimental station at Beaver Lodge, Alberta, and from time to time there has been a great deal of agitation to make it into a full-fledged station. The Minister of Agriculture last summer made a tour of the Peace River and has first-hand information concerning the Beaver Lodge substation. Perhaps he is in a position to tell the committee what the government intends to do so far as the establishment of a station in the Peace River country is concerned. That substation has been operated for a great many years by one who is considered to be fully capable of performing his duties. I understand that he is well known to the minister. Apart from that there are the claims of the people of the Peace River country for a full-fledged station; and since the minister made a tour last summer and acquainted himself with the conditions, he may be in a position now to make a statement concerning this matter.

I did visit this station last summer and found that very valuable work was being carried on there. At the moment I am not in a position to state what the future policy will be with regard to it. I shall foe in a much better position to discuss it when the supplementaries are down. Any provision which is made for such an establishment will have been determined at that time.
I should much prefer to have the discussion deferred until we have the supplementaries down, and if there is an amount for that purpose in the supplementaries we can discuss

Supply-Agriculture-Branch Farms
it from that point of view. But there is an amount in the general estimates for the enlargement of the work that is being done at Beaver Lodge.

That is quite satisfactory. I am quite willing to await the supplementary estimates, provided of course that the minister agrees with me as to the need and desirability of establishing a station in the Peace River country.
There is no question about the need for a station in that vicinity.

I desire to draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and of the committee to a question of great importance to the farmers, especially the horticulturists, of the district of Montreal which, as you know, includes the county of Jacques Cartier. I have received from the district agronomist a letter from which I quote the following paragraph:
The horticulturists of the counties of Jacques Cartier, Laval, Two Mountains, Terrebonne and L'Assomption would like to see the farm at L'Assomption establish a substation either on the island of Montreal or on Jesus island in order to conduct the experiments required by the horticulturists of the district. May I ask the minister to be kind enough to take this matter under consideration?
Shortly, it is this. I have been asked by the horticulturists of my county whether the minister's department would consent to extend the work of the experimental farm at L'Assomption, in the region of the island of Montreal, for the benefit of the horticulturists in that section.

There has been a separate establishment in the black muck area, in the vicinity of Montreal. Some experimental work is being done there. The question whether we should go further with that work is still under consideration. I do not know that I can say any more than that at the moment.

Supply-Agriculture-Branch Farms
The matter is under consideration?
Yes.
Thank you.

I think there are one or two substations or illustration stations in the southern half of Saskatchewan, in what are commonly spoken of as the dried-out areas. I understand that some experiments are being conducted there with respect to controlling soil drifting. Could the minister give us any report on the results of those experiments?

Quite a number of stations have been established throughout the drought area in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta for the purpose of experimenting with ways and means of controlling soil drifting. At some of them, depending on the nature of the district, the idea being promoted is that of strip farming. At others it is the planting of certain types of grasses, or in some cases it is rye in strips two or three feet apart, in order to try to hold the soil and prevent drifting, with the object of getting it regrassed-with the idea not of refarming it but of finding some way of holding and tying it down so that it will not be blowing over on to the next neighbour's land. Then there are other activities in connection with the ridging of the soil, so to speak, in order to gather a moisture supply and hold it. In addition to that, during the last winter at some of these stations they have been ridging the snow, with the idea that, with the drifting that goes on continuously in the west, and the snow always being so light that it sifts along like sand, a ridge of it can be gathered to the extent of two or three feet of snow upon a piece of land. All that is being done to conserve moisture and improve moisture conditions, which in itself tends to hold soil down and prevent drifting. There are activities in other lines, but these are the main ones, and we are getting very good results from them.

Yesterday we were complimenting the officials of the Department of Agriculture upon the splendid work which is being done at the central experimental farm in collaboration with other experimental farms in the development of rust resistant wheat. Is this research work done mostly in Ottawa, so far as the development of rust spores and that kind of thing is concerned?

About half the work
was done at Ottawa, the other half being divided among other places. Some was done in the laboratory at Winnipeg and a certain

amount of work was done at the experimental farm at Indian Head. Some work was also done by the university of Saskatchewan, and at branch farms in western Canada certain experimental work was carried on in regard to production and the following up of the crop during the season.

I wish to say a word
on this vote because the experimental farm at Lennoxville comes under it. I have been through the detailed expenditures of the farm there, and the justification for that farm is the service it can render to the community. They want a certain amount of money. In the supplementary estimates the minister might include another $5,000 for the Lennoxville farm in order to carry further some work that is needed in that section. T would refer particularly to the breeding of horses. We have now one breed, Clydesdale, and there is a growing feeling that Belgians should be included; and if this 85,000 could be brought down in the supplementary estimates for experimental farms and added to the budget of the Lennoxville farm, which by the way is rendering excellent service to the community, it would be of considerable benefit to all the people there.

There is, I believe,
about $4,000 of an increase included in the general estimates for the Lennoxville farm. I cannot say at the moment what, if anything, wdll be in the supplementaries. They will probably be before the house in a few days.
May I express approbation of the work done on the experimental farms and offer a word of encouragement to the minister to go forward, extending the activities of these farms.

Item agreed to.
Science services administration, $25,435.

I understand that rust
work is carried on at Winnipeg. Have they proper greenhouse facilities?

There are greenhouse
facilities at Winnipeg, but it is a question whether they are as extensive as they ought to be. We could always use increased space, but within the estimates that we have seen fit to bring before the house we have made provision for all the space we can just now.

I have not asked the minister any questions in connection with his estimates, but under this item of science services, which is the most important one I see in the whole of the estimates for agriculture, I would ask him what he is doing

Supply-Agriculture-Science Services
for planned agricultural development for the next twenty-five years. After reading all that has been said, I cannot see that the minister has taken any steps to avail himself of the great opening in England to-day not only for new storage facilities underground, but for marketing, and other features of supplying the mother country with food in days of stress and strain. In the second place, I should like to see under this scientific department a closer cooperation than there has been between agriculture and industry. Last year I said:
I would like to see a maximum production of farm products, and would also like to see a close cooperation between agricultural and industrial producers; for the great and extensive needs of agriculture must be supplied. Prosperous industry depends upon a prosperous agriculture, and the Conservative party has always been associated with the development of agriculture. It is one industry which has not rallied to communist propaganda. I should like to see agriculture in Canada developed by a comprehensive plan, and one which would be adapted to Canada's situation. That could be done by the collaboration of the provincial representatives of agricultural departments with people concerned with industry, and in that way the whole rural population of Ontario would be lifted to a higher collective life. It could be done, not by ruining anybody but by merging single interests into one united national endeavour to develop agriculture in all its forms. In that way we would lift our country to a higher economic and social plane. Every individual should be engaged in this work.
I do not believe that there has been much development in the scientific field of agriculture. The British Minister of Agriculture has had an elaborate inquiry made into this very important question, .because agriculture is failing to-day. In this connection I wish to read one or two paragraphs from an article that I came across recently. They apply to Canada's position at the present time. Canada should be supplying the mother country and collaborating with her in the scientific development of agriculture. This article is headed Waste Not, Want Not, and appears in the May issue of the great National Review. It deals with agriculture in the dominions and indicates how the dominions can help the mother country not only at the present time but in times of war and stress. Referring to Canada's scientific development of farming the writer says:
In the Dominion of Canada the fisheries are a declining factor, consequent on the application of a maximum of mechanical aids and a minimum of human power. The prairies in the central regions are losing their fertility in an endeavour to supply wheat for exportation with a maximum of machine power, and a minimum of man power; and the same sequence applies to timber or mineral productions. Over eighty per cent of Canada's exportations are basic raw materials or primary products, and the whole
population of this vast extent of the earth's surface is only in the neighbourhood of 11,000,000.
The point which I wish to make clear is that during the last decade, since machinery in the dominion has been employed in geometrical progression towards the destruction of primary natural resources for export, the country has failed to increase in man power. Not only is this the case, but the problem of unemployment is probably as acute in Canada as elsewhere. The same reasoning holds to a more or less degree when applied to other parts of the British Empire from which countries, dominated by industrialism or relentless machine economy, derive their supplies of raw materials. . . .
Despite the Ottawa agreements the outer industrialized world derives infinitely more of its supplies of raw materials from the British Empire than does the United Kingdom. The avowed policy of Japan, Germany, or other countries which clamour for primary products is dictated solely by interests of industrialization or machine economy, and could not fail to have a further sterilizing effect on the growth of British dominions and colonies in population power.
The truth is that the mechanisms begin to exhaust the world's stock of raw materials, and most of the troubles in modern countries under the aegis of machine economy result from a gradually widening deficit of this supply of primary products. . . .
Scientific pundits tell us that they can create a thousand articles out of cow's milk, and india-rubber out of lime, and coal. But, fundamentally they cannot make something out of nothing, and that great metaphysical problem remains. In reality the scientist creates nothing; all he does is to transform one material substance into another; and a spider in the corner can do that without mathematical formulae, test tubes, or extraneous primary products. The scientifically minded, who sport the cap and bells of modern thought in most countries, assume that their transformations of man's natural environment into a state of artificial mechanical flux, wherein man will ultimately find no abiding place, must continue uncontrolled and unchecked. They constantly reiterate that this is progress, and the millenium is around the corner; but to my mind it is not progress which denudes the world's surface and at the same time tends to extinguish human personality and human fecundity. It is not progress which leaves vast areas of the world's surface destitute of natural resources and barren of inhabitants, condemns millions of people to wallow in the misery of forced unemployment, or flings them into the trough of modern war as cannon fodder.
As has been said in that article, " Waste not, Want Not" is not only true in England, but has a special application to the Canadian prairies. I have a number of the reports. I do not wish to be unfair to the minister, but he ought to do something to relieve this situation. Many farmers are going to the United States. For example, we have farms around the city of Toronto; scientific agriculture should not apply only to the prairies; there should be equality of treatment in connection with all these estimates. The minister should consider the suburban areas



Supply-Agriculture-Science Services
of Canada scientifically and in every other way. My hon. friends from the west urge a great many problems upon the house; but they forget all about the suburban worker, the truck farmer and many other classes, and transportation which would lower the cost of living. These are very important features. I hope that during the recess the minister will collaborate with the British scientists I have named and with the British government to see what coordination there can be between Canada and the mother country. Do hon. members know that at Easter in 1918 the mother country had only two days' supply of food? She has to import 80 per cent of her food and 100 per cent of her raw material. If a crisis came again, as in 1914, she could be starved out, because she has 3,000 fewer ships to-day than she had in 1914.

One of the chief ideas we had in mind in sending to London this year a man with some scientific as well as practical knowledge of Canadian agriculture, and one who was himself born in England and had his earliest education there, was to take care of such a situation which has been mentioned. We felt that a man with that experience in different parts' of Canada, the United States, and Great Britain, and with a scientific and technical knowledge of agriculture as well, would be in a position to do just such things as it has been stated should be done.
Much of the scientific work in relation to agricultural production is carried on in cooperation with such institutions as agricultural colleges, and the provincial departments of agriculture. Outside of the drought area work the distribution of funds expended for these purposes can properly be said to have been made fairly across Canada. In fact it will be found that most of those expenditures were made in the central part of Canada. That is only natural because much of the fruit and vegetable growing and work having to do with the kind of agriculture particularly concerned is carried on in that section of Canada.

While I appreciate that a very excellent work is being done in the experiments carried on at these experimental stations and the central experimental farm, I still fear that we are building up a great white elephant requiring ever-increasing expenditure, and that agriculture is not deriving benefit in proportion to the amount being spent. Our expenditures are far too great for the benefits we receive, great as those benefits have been. This work could be done in such a way as to benefit the
[Mr. Church.)
farmers, without being so elaborate and expensive. No one can examine into the experimental stations and the central experimental farm or the agricultural colleges without being struck by the fact that there is a great deal of unnecessary expenditure from which agriculture derives no benefit.

I am inclined to think that if the words just spoken by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson) are true it is not because the work which is being done by the experimental farms is not valuable, but because of a trip-up somewhere else in our national economy, as a result of which our farm people are unable to derive benefit from the findings of agricultural research. I am sympathetic with the view of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). I believe we are neglecting altogether too much the consistent development of our agricultural productive power. I fear it is falling into decay. I said something about that the other night, and I do not wish to over-elaborate it; but what might happen should we be subjected to a grave international crisis, with our agricultural productive plant more or less depleted, has been cause for great concern to me. I do not wish now to make any suggestions as to practical steps to be taken, but I feel that the question we were discussing to some extent yesterday afternoon, that of stabilizing prices, making it possible for the farmer to produce, with a fair assurance of profit, swine, butter, eggs and other products, would be a very proper one upon which to centre our attention. I do not wish to say too much about this, but we may come to the point where it will be found altogether in the national interest to subsidize some agricultural industries, either by direct subsidy or by some sort of arrangement with the railways for a decrease in freight rates, or in some other manner to make sure that our agricultural productive plant shall be maintained. The articles read by the hon. member for Broadview indicate that there is growing alarm throughout the empire concerning this question. I commend the minister for his activities. In my judgment he has carried on his work this year with a high degree of efficiency and vision. I wish to assure him that he will receive no opposition from our part of the house when he undertakes to enlarge the activities of his department and go forward in strengthening Canada agriculturally.

As the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson) has said, there appears to be an enormous amount of money being spent, and I accept his point of view as an experienced farmer that it is not produc-

Supply-Agriculture-Science Services
ing adequate results. I notice that the total expenditure under the head of agriculture for the year 1936-37 was 31,117,000, and this year it is up to 39,160,000. Is that just because the treasury is receiving more money? Is it not true that much of this work is being duplicated in the different provinces? It is all the money of the public, just the same. I think the hon. member's point is well taken, that there is a good deal of money needlessly spent and without result. From a business point of view there should be much greater economy in this respect on the part of the federal government and the provincial governments as well.

The figures given by the hon. member in regard to the expenditure are not the correct ones. He compares the estimates of last year and this year, but the expenditure last year was 39,266,476 on the two items we have been considering in the general estimates, as will be seen at the bottom of page 5. The estimated total this year is 39,160,532, which is smaller than the total expenditure of last year, but as yet of course we have not dealt with the supplementary estimates for this year. It is possible that there may be a slightly larger expenditure this year when the supplementaries are brought down, but there will not be anything like the increase which has been indicated.
May I ask the minister to explain the increase of 319,396 under this item?

This is the new branch of the department; that is, we have taken the science services of the different branches and put them all under one head, and of course there is a new administration set-up in connection with that, only part of which existed previously, which accounts for some of this increase. This year permanent salaries amount to 310,280, as against 34,959 last year. Temporary salaries amount to 34,155 this year as against $1,080 last year. In those two items there is an increase of 38,396. Then there are several new items: supplies, 3500; printing and stationery, $2,000; travelling expenses, $3,000 and miscellaneous, $500. Those are all new. There is also provision for cooperative investigations, amounting to $5,000; that is new as well. These are the new services in the branch which has been set up.

Last evening I intimated that if a comparison of the expenditures of the Department of Agriculture with those of the other departments were made, serious discrepancies might be disclosed. Yesterday we listened to a very well prepared speech by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) which I think should stand him in good stead
at the forthcoming national convention of his party. Criticism was levelled at the Department of Agriculture and the minister at present responsible for its administration. It will be recalled that the hon. member for Greenwood recommended that the standard of Canadian live stock be raised by direct assistance to the farmers; that new and permanent markets for Canadian products be found, and that farming be made more profitable. I submit that the department is positively taking steps in that direction. Having been connected with farming either directly or indirectly all my life it is my opinion that this government, and the present Department of Agriculture, have done more to promote the interests of agriculture in a practical, scientific manner than any other department or government since confederation. The policies of agricultural trade expansion and general assistance to agriculture have been most effective during the past three years. The great increase in exports of agricultural products to the United States, to European countries and to Great Britain has in large measure restored the confidence of the Canadian farmer. Improvements in breeding, feeding, housing and the marketing of Canadian bacon hogs have been greatly facilitated by the information which has been placed at their disposal. The instructions and advice that have been given in connection with dairy products have increased the quality and quantity as well as the price. The development of seed grain and its distribution to areas for which it is best adapted has been promoted in a very excellent manner. Inspection, grading, packing and shipping facilities in respect of farm products have resulted in great improvement during the last few years. Dairy herds and soils have been more extensively tested, and I am most grateful to the officials of the department and to the minister for the work that has been and is being done in the constituency which I have the honour to represent in this house.
I am not intimating or suggesting that everything that is necessary has been done. I do submit, however, that commensurate with economic conditions and the available staff, rapid progress has been made in almost every direction. In conclusion I desire to give credit where credit is due.

I was very much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Duffus); it is very interesting to learn that the department is operating so successfully in his part of the country, but I do not think we in the maritime provinces have been blessed with the same benefits.

I should like to ask a question in connection with the potato crop of the maritime provinces. As the minister knows, we have been having great difficulty in marketing our potatoes during the last few years, and those interested in the industry have been looking for other outlets. One of the outlets that I understood was being experimented with was the possibility of using potatoes for the production of industrial alcohol, which I think would come under this item. I should like to ask the minister what success his department has had in the production of industrial alcohol from potatoes; if it is of any economic value to the farmers, and whether or not these experiments are being carried on at the present time.

There is an experiment being carried on in connection with the production of alcohol from potatoes, but as yet it has not been determined that alcohol can be produced commercially in that way; that is, in a way that would permit its being used to advantage as against other kinds of alcohol, or, if it is to be used for fuel, in such a way that it could be used as against other types of fuel.
The main service that has been given by this branch has 'been in connection with the study and treatment of diseases of the potatoes of the maritime provinces and other similar crops. There has been an inspection service furnished also, which assists- in marketing the crop in the central part of Canada. As far as this particular vote is concerned the investigation into the production of alcohol from potatoes, as well as the treatment of diseases, is being carried on just as actively as anywhere else.
Then the idea has not been abandoned that it may be of value at some time?
No, the idea has not been abandoned, but we have not yet reached a point where we can report it as commercially possible.

The temporary and permanent appointments are made under the Civil Service Act. Those who receive wages are taken on from day to day.

Bacteriology, $39,670.
I understand that there have been some activities under this vote in connection with the dairy industry of British Columbia.

The activities include the study of problems arising in the processing of milk, in the manufacture of butter, cheese, ice cream, condensed milk, dehydrated milk, casein, milk sugar, fermented milks and by-products, and bacteriological, chemical and other research work for the purpose of establishing sound principles of manufacture in the dairy industry. The group confers with and advises dairymen and managers of dairies and milk product factories in regard to new problems requiring scientific treatment. It is also called upon to ascertain and develop the most appropriate methods to be applied in the making of high grade and uniform dairy products and to investigate and apply remedial measures to new defects which arise from time to time in manufactured products.
Work has been carried on in British Columbia particularly with regard to wood taint and surface deterioration in the storage of butter. The matter of wood taint and surface deterioration in connection with the storage of export butter has become a problem

of serious economic importance to the Canadian butter industry and studies have been and are still being undertaken to determine ways and means of overcoming these defects. The moisture content of boxes, the type of wood, the length of storage period, the temperature of storage and the methods of packing have been studied. They have not arrived at a solution of that particular problem?
The proper type of box lining is considered a solution.

expenditure is made under this item. I am not finding any fault with the work done by the department in an endeavour to control the infestation of grasshoppers, cutworms and so on. To what extent does

I am not getting on my feet, Mr. Chairman, to condemn the entomological branch, because they are doing a splendid service, but I do condemn the increase I see in the ten items on this page of approximately 8300,000.

My hon. friend may have had experience in other lines. It is a shame that we are wasting so much money on experimental farms. If you had smaller farms spread all over the country they would give the public greater service, but here you have this great, big expensive farm at Ottawa, and only a few years ago, when the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) was Minister of Agriculture, we bought the old Booth farm to add to the central experimental farm-

In answer to the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), there was a severe outbreak of the cutworm in a certain section of New Brunswick last year. A small infestation developed during 1937, but substantially no crop was destroyed in the greater part of the area infested. An annual survey is made of the abundance and life history and cultural conditions which make for outbreaks of this insect, and this helps in curbing it.

Two or three years ago a new kind of insect appeared that infested apples. It was called the apple maggot, and for a while there was grave danger that it would interfere with our export market because the regulations against infected apples going into the United Kingdom were very strict. I
tMr. Spenoe.1
wonder what progress has been made in eliminating that pest. It appeared in certain sections of Ontario as well as in Nova Scotia.

The maggot is in
existence. An attempt has been made to get it under control, and while its prevalence has been considerably decreased it has not been completely wiped out.

It threatened to make very serious trouble for our apples in the British market. Another insect which infected peaches appeared in the Niagara peninsula two or three years ago, and its ravages threatened for a short time to be very destructive. I wonder if the minister could say to what extent that pest is being controlled.

The oriental peach moth has been creating some trouble, but there is a parasite which has pretty well cleaned it up. The shipment of our apples to Great Britain is protected against infestation of maggots through our inspection system. A very close check is kept of all apples that go out of a district which is infected with the maggot.
What progress has been made in controlling the warble fly? It is of considerable importance in our section of the province.

What cooperation is there between provincial governments and the federal department in connection with these scientific services?

There is very close cooperation between the officials of the federal department and any officials provincially employed in agricultural colleges, schools and elsewhere; but the greater part of the expense of this service is carried by the federal department.

Yesterday I mentioned an investigation into the destruction caused by the pea moth, and the minister said he would give me some information when we reached this item. I wish he would tell the committee something about the activities of his department in the lower mainland of British Columbia, and what results have been obtained in controlling the pea moth.

I have a memorandum here on the pea moth:
The pea moth continues to be of serious import in the pea-growing areas of Gaspe, Quebec, and the lower Fraser valley, British Columbia. In both areas, however, the pest was at somewhat less than its usual abundance,

the loss in Gaspe for the whole district being about one per cent, and in the most severely infested districts approximately ten per cent, with many growers, however, being unable to continue the growing of peas for market.
The same is substantially true in the lower Fraser Valley where in large districts dried pea growing has practically stopped due to the infestations in the past. An entirely satisfactory control has not yet been worked out, though certain cultural operations and oil emulsion sprays in British Columbia and the selection of sites for the pea plantings in the Gaspe country indicate that the infestations can be very materially, if not entirely eliminated, thus effecting a saving of many thousands of dollars to the industry.
That is a short review of what has taken place. There has not been any great progress made in meeting the infestation.

Practically all of that
increase in temporary staff is due to the infestation of sawfly in the lumbering areas. In cooperation with the lumber industry, we are attempting to meet that infestation. Most of the additional expenditure for temporary employment is for that purpose.

Well, hasn't anything
been done in that direction in the past?
Yes, something has been done in the past, but the infestation is growing more widespread and more difficult to handle, and we think a real attack should be made on it.

I should
like to mention the very valuable services of the entomological station at Fredericton, New Brunswick. Our city is particularly noted for the elm shade trees along the streets. A pest attacked those trees, particularly last year, and Mr. Balch, the head entomologist at Fredericton, from his research was able to show what would eradicate it. His advice has been taken by the city, and it is expected that as a result the trees will be saved. Not only shade trees but the forest trees are being cared for through the advice and information given by the departmental officers at Fredericton.
Have arrangements been made for improving the building occupied by the entomological branch at Fredericton? It is located on the campus of the university of New Brunswick.
A mistake from an architectural standpoint was made in an addition to it, and situated as it is, that mistake should be corrected. It would not cost very much. The matter has been taken up with the department, but no progress has been made. I am sure that it would be in the interests of the department to see that that mistake is corrected.

I can only say that there is no amount in these estimates to take care of any improvement at Fredericton, but the matter is under consideration, and when the supplementaries are down we shall be in a better position to discuss it.

What steps have been taken in the province of New Brunswick for the control or elimination of the sawfly. The minister a moment ago made some mention of the matter; I wonder if his statement could be made more complete?

The headquarters of the forest insect investigation work is at Ottawa, but there is a branch laboratory at Fredericton which takes charge of that work in New Brunswick and the Gaspe peninsula. The headquarters for the parasite work is at Belleville. There has been imported into Canada a parasite which destroys the sawfly, and this year 70,000,000 of these parasites were distributed. The Belleville plant not only has imported the parasite but multiplies them there, and distribution is made to different places, including New Brunswick.
What can the minister report with regard to the infestation by other insects than sawfly affecting the other conifers -the tamarack in the west, and the spruce and the red pine?

The two chief parasites are the larch sawfly, which is being dealt with through a parasite in much the same way as the other sawfly-and I understand that a distribution of that parasite has been made in British Columbia to deal with the larch saw-fly-and the bark beetle. There is a method available of dealing with the bark beetle, and anyone communicating with the branches concerned can get information in that regard.
Would the minister gather that the infestation is growing rapidly? Is it sweeping up through the north, or what do the surveys indicate?
We have . no definite report on that. We are not in a position to say whether or not it is extending northward.

Item agreed to.
Canadian travel bureau service-to assist in promoting tourist business in Canada, $250,000.
Can the minister give a brief description of the work done by the travel bureau? What is the size of the staff?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) :
speechtext:
The amount asked for is to provide for the administration of the Canadian travel bureau for the fiscal year 1938-39. Further extension of Canada's tourist business is an essential part of the work of national development and indicates a clear way in which Canada can largely increase its national revenue. Practically every country is now recognizing the tourist traffic as a main item of trade, and the matter of attracting tourist travel has become a highly competitive business, with the governments of various countries either directly or indirectly carrying on tourist promotional work. Of this amount of $250,000 approximately $185,000 will be utilized for direct advertising in newspapers and magazines. Of this amount approximately $165,000 will be spent in advertising in United States papers and periodicals. The United States is the country from which Canada draws by far the greater number of its tourists, and approximately ninety-five per cent of the tourist expenditure in Canada is by tourists from the United States. That country is, however, the object of aggressive tourist propaganda by every other leading tourist country; consequently if Canada is to extend its present tourist travel from that country, or even to hold it, it is necessary that the stimulation of interest in the recreational attractions of the dominion be strenuously continued. During 1937 the bureau carried advertisements amounting to 302 insertions in sixty-three newspapers in the larger cities and 127 insertions in fifty magazines, most of them with nation-wide circulation.

Supply-Transport-Travel Bureau
During the year 1937 the bureau received a total of 75,196 inquiries as compared with 52,668 received in 1936, an increase of 42-7 per cent. Of these 75,196 inquiries 66,207, or 88 per cent, were the result of direct advertising.
This year we are devoting about $25,000 to the initiation of a campaign in the British isles, and we are already receiving very satisfactory returns therefrom. The campaign is carried out under the supervision of Canada House and under the immediate supervision of the Hon. Vincent Massey, high commissioner. This is a new departure, and if the results after the tourist season warrant, we may ask the house next year for an increase in the vote. To-day, we regard the effort in Great Britain as largely experimental.
The bureau has nine of a permanent staff, and during the tourist season, the rush season, we have a temporary staff of nine more.

I take it from what the minister has just said, and also from the report of the department, that the work of the bureau is largely publicity, advertising, publications and work of that sort. I wonder whether the minister has read that portion of the report of the national employment commission, the Purvis commission, dealing with the tourist business. We have had so many repoi'ts this year that perhaps he has not read that particular one, but I would call his attention to a suggestion contained on page 10 of the Purvis report. Referring to the tourist trade the report states:
Because the trade benefits all the people of Canada, and because tourists visit Canada, not provinces of Canada, and tour at will across provincial boundaries, the commission is of the opinion that the dominion government might be well advised to bring about a coordinated national effort to stimulate the tourist trade.
In other words, that the dominion might give national leadership in building up the tourist business. The report goes on:
To this end the commisison recommends that the dominion government set up a national advisory tourist committee, representative of all the provinces, to advise governmental and other interested bodies respecting policies and administration of such phases of the tourist trade as come within their respective jurisdictions or as may be deemed wise to be brought under dominion jurisdiction, such advisory committee to be composed of a minister from each provincial government, a limited number of citizens interested in developing Canada's resources as attractions, representatives of the Canadian Association of Tourist and Publicity Bureaux, together with one or more ministers of the dominion government.
That seems like a reasonable suggestion. Has anything along that line been done by the government? I take it action would come under the Canadian travel bureau.

The purpose of this vote,
which was initiated in 1934, is exactly that described by the hon. gentleman. It was never its purpose to do all the travel advertising of the dominion. It has been set up for the purpose of coordinating the work of other agencies. Each province spends a considerable appropriation for the same purpose, each of our railways has appropriations much larger than this, and our steamship companies also have appropriations. The purpose of this vote is to coordinate the efforts of all agencies in the dominion seeking to develop the tourist trade, and to this work the dominion bureau is largely confined. The bureau directs the advertising; usually an advertisement from the dominion bureau is accompanied by one or more of other Canadian advertisements, either of provinces or of the railways. The purpose of including the federal advertising is that if the other advertisement does not meet a particular need it is apparent to anyone reading the advertising that there is a central agency at Ottawa from which information about any part of the dominion may be obtained. The principal work of the dominion bureau is to act as a clearing house. Provinces which receive inquiries relating to districts beyond their own areas forward them to the dominion bureau.
It is my own opinion after closely observing the situation that tourist development as far as advertising goes is highly technical work. The director of our branch works with directors of other agencies. It is an association of technical men, and it is my opinion that the situation could not be greatly improved by adding to that group men who have only a general knowledge of the subject, as suggested in the Purvis report.
At the present time there is no such thing as a national advisory tourist committee. Would it not help if some such committee were set up?

At every dominion-provincial conference the ministers concerned with tourist traffic discuss the matter. I have attended two such conferences, and I think they meet the need. I doubt very much whether duplicating as a dominion affair the travel bureaux found in every city in Canada would be much help. I should not be disposed to take the initiative in setting up the sort of organization my friend suggests.

Every detail of that work is carried on under the proper department of government. For example, our national parks provide for the sale of Canadian products for tourists visiting the parks. The government is assisting in the construction of highways, has done so for many years and will probably continue to do so. I see no purpose in putting any of that work under the direction of a tourist bureau, which is formed for an entirely different purpose, that of directing travellers to the attractions of Canada. The creation of the attractions is being adequately taken care of by the proper department of government.

My idea is that the Canadian travel bureau should head up the development of the tourist business right across Canada. This report states that the value of the tourist business to Canada is over 1300,000,000 a year. Perhaps the minister will not dispute that figure.
Not at all.

I suggest that he give these recommendations serious consideration. In the report of the bureau itself for the fiscal year 1936-37, at page 112 of the annual report of the Department of Transport, we find this statement:
Particularly interesting were the large number of inquiries regarding a trip across Canada, and a small folder descriptive of the trans-Canada highway trip was issued to provide information on this subject.
I have the folder on the trans-Canada highway trip. It bears the name of the minister and the deputy minister, but the automobile trip includes 250 miles by boat across lake Superior from Sault Ste. Marie to Fort William, and another 90 miles by rail

in British Columbia where the Big Bend highway should be and is not. I have asked two ministers already what the present position is with regard to the trans-Canada highway, where gaps are still uncompleted. Could the minister give the committee that information?
My friend has given it himself. There is an uncompleted part between Schreiber and somewhere in the Michipicoten area, about 250 miles in extent.
That is the 250 miles mentioned in this pamphlet, the water trip between Sault Ste. Marie and Fort William. That does not refer to the uncompleted portion of the highway.

The uncompleted portion is
less than 250 miles-about 100 miles. I think work is proceeding at both ends to join in the middle. In the Big Bend section in British Columbia there is a gap, but work is being done there, divided, I think, between the Department of Natural Resources and the British Columbia government.

When is it expected that
the uncompleted part in northern Ontario will be finished? Is any definite effort being made to close it up quickly? It seems to me that both this government and the previous government have been very slow about getting the trans-Canada highw'ay completed.

As my hon. friend knows,
the provinces have control of the highways, and allocate the funds, their own and the contribution of this government, as they see fit. I think both provinces are making an effort to close the gaps, and we are assisting them to do so.

Can the minister indicate
when it is expected that the gap in northern Ontario will be closed?

I am not in a position to
say that at the moment.

This tourist vote has been
the same for several years, and the industry is becoming increasingly important. Is the minister satisfied that the vote is large enough?

We should like at least a
million dollars; I am sure my staff could spend it very well. Since the tourist vote was inaugurated the tourist business has about trebled, so we think excellent results are being obtained with the present vote.

Surely you are not taking
credit for all that?

My director claims credit
for every new tourist coming in.

Supply-Transport-Pensions
Of the funds contributed by the dominion government is any amount earmarked for any particular highway?

All funds of that kind are
spent under an agreement between the dominion and the provinces. An agreement is made each season, and the funds are allocated to different projects.

When does the minister expect the road to be finished between Jasper and lake Louise? That will be one of the finest scenic highways on the North American continent. Thousands of tourists anticipate taking a motor trip through that country as soon as it is finished.

The work on that road is
under the Department of Mines and Resources, the estimates of which will be brought down shortly, and the minister of that department can give a better answer than I. But I know it is expected that it will be finished.
Do the provinces contribute to the development or maintenance of our national parks?

Not the national parks. The federal parks are the sole property of the federal government, and all expenditures are made by this government. There are, however, some provincial parks where the opposite is true; all expenditures are made by the provinces. The federal parks are maintained by the federal government.
What are the functions and duties of the official listed as an investigator in the travel bureau?

Our department is constantly extending its list of tourist potentialities, and the investigator visits new roads that have been opened up or new sports resorts and places of that kind in order to collect information which may be sent out by the bureau in pamphlets or otherwise to tourists, and generally acts as a sort of development man for the industry.

Item agreed to.
Pensions and other benefits-Railway employees provident fund-
To supplement pension allowances under the provisions of the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railway employees provident fund Act so as to make the minimum payment during the period January 1, 1938 to March 31, 1939, the sum of $30 per month instead of $20 as fixed by the said act, $26,300.

No doubt the minister is just as familiar as I am with the terms under which Prince Edward Island entered confederation. The word " efficient " was used in the contract under which they came into confederation, and they were also guaranteed continuous communication with the Intercolonial railway and the railway system of the dominion. It appears to me that during the greater part of the year there is no efficient service provided, and there certainly is not the continuous communication that was promised. I feel that we in this parliament are obligated by the contract entered into between the fathers of confederation and those representing the island. It may be that the service given to-day compares favourably with what was promised in 1873; but we have gone ahead considerably, and I do not think the connections between the island and the mainland are of that degree of efficiency and provide that continuity of communication which was contemplated when Prince Edward Island entered confederation.
I understand that in certain seasons, if you leave Montreal on the train that leaves around the noon hour, you are likely to have a wait of twenty hours at Sackville before you can make ferry connections to the island. That information was given to me by a gentleman who should know the conditions existing. He lives on the island and is actively associated with the board of trade in Charlottetown. He did not intend that this information should have any political significance. I do not want to discuss this item at any length, but I do want to lay this suggestion before the minister. I have not had as much time as I should like to have had to digest the information. It came in the mail only the day before yesterday, but it looks as though a serious effort should be made to live up to our contract to

Sup-ply-Transport-Steamships
provide ways and means of making the means of communication to and from the island more readily available.
The population of the island is shrinking, and I sometimes wonder if this is not due to our neglect of the opportunities to be found there. It is only an island, but it is one of the provinces of this dominion. I do not' like to make comparisons between provinces because I remember what a certain author said about comparisons, but I do feel that the people of Prince Edward Island have put up with conditions that the people of other provinces would not put up with. It may be that they feel they have had to do this because their population is shrinking and they have not the voice in the affairs of the dominion that other provinces have. I know, if the hon. members from the island were present, they would associate themselves with me when I make the suggestion that we should do something. It would not cost a great deal of money to provide better travel facilities between the island and the mainland.
In the railway committee I suggested that the railway connections should be speeded up in order to assist tourist traffic and industry in general. The island has no great number of industries, but it is a rich farming country. I believe its farming population could be increased if conditions were more favourable. I also believe we could stop the shrinkage in the population and perhaps bring about an increase. I do not criticize the department or the minister; I am simply doing my duty to the island that was the cradle of confederation. I think we owe this to the island from the historic and economic point of view. I agree that the ferry service from the cape to the island could be quite good if the railway company would do its share and cooperate a little more in connecting with the ferries. But that is only in the summer months. For eight months in the year travel is made difficult through lack of proper facilities to get to and from the island and to make the proper connections with the railways. I leave this suggestion with the minister in the hope that it will receive the consideration it deserves. I feel sure the minister knows it deserves consideration. I do not want my remarks to be taken merely as criticisms directed at the department or the government.

The power company are now building two storage dams off our property altogether in branch streams, and it is expected that when they are finished they will be able to regulate the levels there so that there will always be water available for power purposes.

The principle of central control of Canada's national harbours has now been in effect considerably over two years. At first the administration was under a temporary board, but since October 1, 1936, the permanent board appointed pursuant to the provisions of the National Harbours Board Act has been in charge.
Without going into details of the many steps taken by the board to improve the position of our national harbours both from the point of view of efficiency and dispatch and from the financial standpoint, I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to a few figures indicating the substantial and gratifying progress which has been made thus far.
Taking each of the harbours that have been administered under the new system throughout the past two years, and comparing the results in 1937 with the situation in 1935,

Speaking generally, the result of two years' operation under the principle of national central control of national harbours may be stated thus: In 1935, the last year the harbours were under the administration of local commissions, aggregate operating revenues stood at $7,427,454.77. Mr. Chairman, may I speak to the committee, and especially to the minister, about the port of Montreal? As we all know, the port of Montreal is of vital interest to the whole Dominion of Canada.

As the minister is aware, for over fifty years it has been the custom at the port of Montreal, and I assume also at the port of Quebec, although as to the latter port I am saying only what I believe to be the case, to levy certain charges for lifting the grain from the canal boats into the elevator and certain charges for delivering the grain out of the elevator into the ocean boats, the charges being split between the two boats concerned. In the early history of these ports, particularly the port of Montreal, this charge was half a cent a bushel, and at that time it was equally divided between the lake boats and the ocean boats. To-day, of course, on account of the increased costs, the charge per bushel has also increased, so that we have a total charge of $10.25 per 1,000 bushels. This $10.25 is apportioned between the lake boat and the ocean boat as follows: $6.25 per 1,000 bushels is payable by the lake boat when the grain is unloaded, and $4 per 1,000 bushels is payable by the ocean boat when the grain is delivered to it.
In addition to the service which the elevator performs of unloading the grain from the lake boat and delivering it to the ocean boat, it stores the grain free of charge for a period of ten days. After that, there is a charge of so much per bushel according to a rate schedule in operation at the present time. The service of loading and unloading has apparently worked very satisfactorily in the ports of Montreal and Quebec over a period of fifty years. I want to emphasize this point again: It would have been discrimination against the port of Montreal and eventually discrimination against the grain growers of western Canada if this rate had been put into effect. Action was deferred until a certain date. Then, after further protests, it was further deferred until November 13 of this year. The season does not close until December 1. The minister made the statement that this rate of $4 per 1,000 bushels would not be collected from the grain during this season; yet the agreement with the grain brokers and shipowners of Montreal expires November 13, and the rate goes into effect after that date. I think the minister will agree that my information is correct in this instance.

It was determined that there was absolutely no contract outstanding beyond November 13. If any shipper wishes to have the steamer pay his elevation after November 13, all he has to do is write it into the charter.

I know the grain brokers of Montreal will be happy to have the intimation from the minister that there will be no change in the assessment of that $4 per 1,000 bushels during the course of the current shipping season.
I would not bother to convey that information because I do not think they would value my hon. friend's information on that point. I never saw a man with less background for work of this kind.
Well, now-

They have a high regard for the Minister of Transport. If the Minister of Transport considers that I have no background for a discussion of this kind, I am sorry he has formed such an opinion. On many occasions I could have made the same suggestion, but I would not do it. I have a high regard for the Minister of Transport and I hope he has the same for me. If his attitude is the condition which must prevail in this committee; if we must carry on debates in that frame of mind, I am not unwilling to carry on in that way. I am willing to take my share of abuse along with any other member of this house.
There is no necessity for abuse.

The minister has suggested that no grain was diverted. I grant that there has been none diverted yet because of the arrangements that have been made, but there will be if something is not done to adjust them. I still want to emphasize this fact: Why was it necessary to make this change in a custom that had prevailed for fifty years? This had worked satisfactorily, but suddenly there is a diversion of this S4 charge from the ship to the grain owner. Why not leave things in status quo when they have been working so satisfactorily? The minister suggests that next year the rates on tramp steamers carrying grain will be lowered to cover this charge of $4 per 1,000 bushels. Why not leave matters alone when things are going along satisfactorily? Why make a change? When nothing is to be gained, why

Supply-Transport-Harbours Board
break a custom that has prevailed in this port for many years? If we were to have increased revenues as a result of this change, then I would say, make it, but there is nothing being accomplished this year except disturbance. I do not think the Minister of Transport should countenance a change of this kind simply for the sake of making a change. Changes are not always good; some are bad. I consider that this change is unnecessary. I believe it will work out to the detriment of the port of Montreal. The minister suggested that the harbour commission had no legal right to collect this $4 per
1,000	bushels from the ocean boats. They collect $6.25 per 1,000 bushels from the lake boats.

Let me correct that. They collect only as long as the lake boats agree to pay it. We collect from the parties named in the act, the consignee, the shipper, owner or agent. If some one else pays it, that is simply a matter of arrangement among the parties concerned.

When a lake boat brings down grain they quote the grain broker a rate from the lake port delivered into the elevator at Montreal. That freight rate includes this S6.25 per 1,000 bushels. That has always been done, and it is still being done. That has been the custom for fifty or sixty years, and no change is being made. Apparently it is considered legal for the harbour commission to collect that $6.25.

I am sure my hon. friend
would like to have the facts. Exactly the same change was made in connection with inbound grain as was made in connection with outbound. I shall read the charges again as I think the hon. member should have them in his mind. The old tariff stated that the charge for unloading grain from vessel was payable by the vessel unloaded. That is the charge of $6.25 to which the hon. member is referring. The new tariff states that the charge for unloading grain from vessel is payable on unloading. It does not say by whom it is payable; it simply says it is payable on unloading. The change in connection with outbound grain is exactly the same. The old tariff states that charges in connection with export grain are payable by the vessel unloaded and charges in connection with domestic grain are payable by the shipper. The new tariff states that the charges are payable on loading. It does not say by whom they are payable, any more than in connection with inbound grain. The situation to-day is that the boats pay the inbound charges because they quote a rate

to a shipper or make a charter party which includes the cost of unloading at Montreal. If the charter party includes elevator charges, they will be paid by the ship just the same, but our security for the charge must, under the act, be the grain.

I can only go back to the
statement made by the minister, that it is not legal to do it.
It is not legal to do what?

When the grain is unloaded from a lake vessel into the elevator the Montreal harbour commission makes out a bill against the owner or the agent of the vessel, not against the owner of the grain. But in the case of an ocean vessel, the bill for unloading goes, not to the owner or the agent of the vessel but to the person who has the grain in the elevator. Apparently that is the only difference between the minister and myself, despite my lack of background.

May I correct that? The
account goes to the owner or agent of the grain. We do not care who pays for it because everyone's money looks the same. The owner or the agent of the grain is billed in connection with incoming and outgoing grain.

I have seen a bill which
was sent to the owner of the vessel. When wheat is delivered from a lake boat into the elevator the bill is not made out in the name of the owner of the grain; it is made out in the name of the owner or agent of the vessel and collected as such.

The explanation is that the
owner or agent of the grain has arranged a charter for the lake vessel which includes elevation and has asked the elevator to bill the lake boat as a matter of convenience. But if the lake boat does not pay, the owner of the grain will find a bill in his hands in short order. He is the responsible party under the National Harbours Board Act. There is nothing in the act that states that we can hold a boat responsible for elevation or other charges.

We shall let that point go.
I am perfectly satisfied as to the actual conditions. I believe that the point raised by the grain brokers of Montreal and other points and those interested in the port is well taken. It is unfortunate that all this trouble should have been caused merely for the sake of a bookkeeping entry. After all, that is what it amounts to. In one case one source is held responsible and in another

Supply-Transport-Harbours Board
case, another source is held responsible for the payment of the bill. This custom has existed for fifty years. The minister quoted in connection with the port of Montreal certain figures which showed an increase in freight movement during the first two weeks in April. Naturally those figures speak for themselves, but he must remember that in the early part of April last season there was very little grain shipped through the port of Montreal. The increase shown is not a real increase.

Let me correct that. As a matter of fact shipments of grain in the first two weeks of last year were quite heavy, and there is very little difference between the grain shipments of the first two weeks of this season and the shipments of the first two weeks of last season. The increase is almost wholly in other commodities
Has the minister the figures on that?

I have them in my office. I do not know that I have them here. I get a daily statement, and I am quoting from that. I saw it only this morning, and I think my hon. friend should know the figures because he is making these dogmatic statements.
I am inclined to make dogmatic statements, but the minister is not.
I have the figures before me.
The minister has access to the figures and I have not.
Why make statements if you have not the figures?

I am giving the minister
the information which I have received, which I believe to 'be correct, and it is for others to judge which is the correct information. The minister is in a better position to get the figures than I am. I can get only certain figures, and I am giving them. I cannot agree with the minister; I am sorry I cannot.
He cannot agree, but has he seen the figures?
I have sufficient figures here to show me that this differential of $4-

figures? He is a responsible minister of the crown.

For the first two weeks of the shipping season, 26,759 tons or about 25 per cent, until the end of April. So there is a very slight difference, and I am making a statement which I can verify. This happens to be the statement of May 16.

Would the minister explain in just a few words why, and at whose instigation or suggestion, this change was made?
I have tried to explain-
Just in a very few words.

The very few words are these: Under the old tariff, had a ship refused to pay the charges, we were out our money because we had no legal right to make a ship responsible for the payment of elevation charges. The agent, owner or consignee of the grain are the only people from whom we can legally collect. Why put in the tariff something that you cannot enforce? Why say that a man is responsible for charges when you have no legal right to make him responsible?
Why have you not a legal right to make him responsible when that was the practice which prevailed over a long period of years ?

We are working under the act passed in 1936, and the Department of Justice advises that we have not the legal right to make the ship responsible. We asked for an opinion from the department when we discovered the discrepancy in tariffs, and we were told that we had no legal right to collect from the boat owners if they did not pay of their own free will.
You can refuse clearance to a boat if it refuses to pay.
We cannot collect by legal methods a charge illegally made. You cannot do a thing indirectly, legally, that you cannot do directly.
I am not sure that I have this straight yet. This $4 was formerly charged against the boat owners, illegally, the minister says, and that is why the change was made.
Correct.
And now it will be a charge against the owners of the grain?
Quite.

What I am concerned about is the farmers of the west. Does the minister not think this charge will be levied against the farmer's grain when he sells it to the broker? Does he really not think so?

Supply-Transport-Harbours Board
How many speeches has the hon. member made in his life in which he suggested that all charges, including freight, were made against the farmer?
Quite so.

If we take the S6.25 off the boat carrying the grain down, naturally the freight will be S6.25 less. It is freight plus elevation; that is the way in which rates are quoted and charters are made. Similarly you can look up the rates published by the tramp shipping administration committee in London, and you will find the rate quoted for St. Lawrence ports is the freight rate plus $4 per 1,000 bushels elevation. If it is quoted the other way, these charges will not be included. It will be a flat charge as it always has been from Saint John and Halifax, and if you compare the rates from Saint John and Halifax, you will find that they vary by exactly that four-tenths of a cent per bushel. My hon. friend knows something about grain handling and how rates are charged at country elevators and at Fort William and Vancouver, and he knows that the elevation charges are always assessed against the grain.
I am not clear yet. This $4 that was formerly charged against the boat owners will now be charged against the owner of the grain, who in the first place will be the farmer.
The farmer does not own any grain in Montreal harbour. Of course, my hon. friend may say that all the charges follow the grain, and that is absolutely true.

I was prompted to ask my question because of an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press, which is in pretty close touch with matters of this kind, and I am just giving the committee the effect of that editorial on me. It warned members of parliament to watch when this matter came up in the house, and to get the assurance that this S4 charge would not be levied back against the farmers.
You have that assurance now.

I am glad that my hon. friend was in the house, and I had hoped there would be more western members who would realize my point of view. The minister says that next year this $4 will be seen in a reduction of the freight charges charged by tramp steamers coming into the port of Montreal. On what authority does he make that statement? Has he definite information from the association which fixes the freight rates for tramp steamers plying between different ports, that the freight rate next year 
is going to be reduced S4 from the freight rate charged this year to the port of Montreal? Because if he has not that definite information from the association, the charge will still be there; if it is not taken off the freight rate somebody will have to pay it, and the only person left to pay it is unfortunately the one who supplies the goods that are going to be transported. If the minister can give us a definite statement from the association which controls the freight rates for tramp steamers that they are going to make that reduction, I feel sure that the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) and members from other parts of western Canada will then be in a position to assure the growers of wheat that they need not be nervous about this $4 charge; that it is going to be taken off the freight rate, and that, therefore, it is just a matter of shifting the charge from the freight rate to the owner; that it appears in one column to be taken off another column in the way of reduced freight rates. I should like the minister to give us a definite assurance that he is absolutely certain that this is going to be done.
The rates next year, I am told -and I have every reason to believe it- will be quoted ex-elevation, just as they are quoted to-day with elevation.
They will be $4 less than the actual freight rate this year?
Well, now-
I am sincere, but if the minister cannot understand a proper question-

The hon. member wants me to promise him that rates will be the same or less next year. The differential as between the Atlantic rate and the St. Lawrence river ports rates will be wiped out because the St. Lawrence river ports will no longer carry elevation. The hon. member wants me to say that the rates on tramp tonnage will be the same next year as this year?

No. I want the minister to say that the actual freight rate which tramp steamers are going to charge will be S4 less than the actual freight rate is this year. The minister made a statement to the effect that this was going to be done.
Mr. HOWE; What is the hon. member asking me to say? That the rate a year from now will be S4 per 1,000 bushels less than it is to-day? Is that true?

Yes.

That is not the point. The point the minister made was that I was creating the impression that the western farmer was going to have to pay $4 more, and the minister made the statement that he would not, because the S4 would be off the freight bill.
