And I asked him where his authority was for that. He makes the statement that you cannot guarantee freight rates for next year. I grant that. That is why I doubt whether these tramp steamers will reduce the freight rate next year, despite the statement of the Minister of Transport.

It might be beneficial if we were to go over to the balmy air of the Pacific for a few minutes. I should like to ask the minister what is the present trend with regard to wheat shipments through the port of Vancouver. I believe that almost none of the 1937 crop has been shipped out that way.

There was a certain amount. The situation was disturbed about a year ago or perhaps longer by the abnormally high freight rates. As my hon. friend knows, freight rates soared about 100 per cent on everything, on both the Atlantic and the Pacific. The effect was felt more on the Pacific than on the Atlantic, because the normal rates on the Pacific are higher, and when they double the effect is felt more out there. I am happy to say freights are back to normal or what was considered normal before that increase took place, and as far as anyone can judge we can expect a very large movement of grain through Vancouver this winter, as was usual years ago. At least we think there is no reason why the division of the crop as between movement east and movement west will not apply this year as it applied in other years.
What portion of the 1937 crop was carried through the port of Vancouver?

The 1937 shipments were
23,749,000	bushels. In 1936 they were 64,000,000 bushels; in 1935 46,000.000 bushels; in 1934, 51,000,000 bushels; in 1933, 68,000,000 bushels; but of course a very large part of the reason for that difference is that last
year Saskatchewan had very little wheat to export, and Alberta also had a very small crop. Manitoba, on the other hand, had a good' crop. That would account for some little discrepancy as between the east and the west.

Of course we on the Pacific coast have always felt that, with the line of division running north and south pretty well through Swift Current or Moose Jaw, the quantity of grain shipped through Vancouver should not have decreased so much in the last two years, whereas the amount shipped through Montreal has increased. The figures for Vancouver for 1937, as the minister said, are about
23,700,000	bushels, whereas in 1936 they wore 64,000,000 bushels, and yet we find that for Montreal the figures were 92,600,000 bushels in 1937 and 87,000,000 bushels in 1936. It may be just a coincidence, but those are the years in which the national harbours board has been in charge of our harbours. I do not suppose we can blame them for all the difficulty, but I suggest to the minister that the fact has some significance. Our problems are those of a Pacific port. Ours is the port farthest removed from Ottawa, and I do not believe that sufficient attention is being paid to its future. The members of the board, living here in Ottawa, are not in a position to be in contact with developments on the coast. I suggest to the minister, as I have done at two previous sessions, that there should be a local honorary advisory committee set up in Vancouver, whose main job would be to think of the future of the port and to tackle such a problem as the one which is before us now, namely the reasons why shipments of wheat through Vancouver are falling off, while shipments through the eastern ports are increasing. It may be that the national harbours board could do a great deal to remedy that situation. I ask the minister whether he will not give serious consideration to setting up such a local committee to help the board here in considering the peculiar problems that face us on the Pacific coast.

As regards local advisory boards, a year ago the Canadian chamber of commerce met in Vancouver; one of the resolutions-I received notice of it-was that the chamber should recommend that local advisory boards be established at the principal national ports. The fate of that resolution was very interesting. It never got outside the resolutions committee. The Vancouver members were unanimously against it, according to what I was told-and I made a little analysis because I was rather surprised-Montreal could not carry it by a majority of the

Would the board consider
the erection of a fish dock there? After all, it would serve the fishing fleet and it is very badly needed.
We shall give it very careful consideration after we receive a proposal from the owners of the property.

There are two other difficulties that have occasioned a great deal of trouble in connection with the harbour. One is the lack of police protection. Thousands of dollars worth of goods have been stolen on the harbour front, and probably a good deal of harbour board property has been taken in that way too. The other point is the lack of fire protection. We have yet no fire-boat in the harbour. I raised that point last year. We are still unprotected. What is being done in regard to these two problems?

The city and the harbour

Coming from the Pacific to the Atlantic for a moment, when I listened to the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh) telling us about the wonderful harbour at Montreal and also admitting that there were millions of dollars sunk in that harbour, I was reminded of an item I saw in Seaports for the month of March, written by a travelling	reporter-Activities of a Shipping
Reporter, by Austin F. Cross. That writer was asked the question: "What do you do in winter "? and the thought passed through my mind, What does Montreal do in winter? I can assure the hon. member for Mount Royal that while the harbour of Montreal was covered with twenty-four inches of ice, ice did not prevent the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) from sailing from Halifax overseas, nor did it prevent the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) sailing from Halifax overseas, nor the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) from going

Supply-Transport-Harbours Board
on his recent trip. I would say, therefore, that notwithstanding the glowing description of the port of Montreal, we have in the extreme eastern part of Canada the port of Halifax which is open all the year round. In fact, the harbour is so well known; its advantages are so outstanding, that it does not require a speech in this house to place it where it rightly belongs as the outstanding port of the dominion.
May I now say a few words in regard to the general policy of the national harbours board? The committee will remember that I took strong exception to and was critical of the policy inaugurating a national harbours board under the present system. I took the view that we in the east and the people in the extreme west would not profit to the same extent as would the ports in central Canada. I am inclined to think, looking at the matter from a broad point of view rather than simply from the standpoint of the port of Halifax or of any particular section, that the policy adopted has been a sound one. I say that in all fairness because of my opposition in the past. As a business man I cannot help realizing that the national harbours board under the administration of the present minister has made an exceptionally creditable showing in the past year. When one realizes that the revenue for 1937 amounted to $8,262,221 as compared with $8,030,600 in 1936, or an increase of $231,621, showing an increase of three per cent as a revenue producer, and when one realizes further that the expenditures in connection with operations showed a decrease of $226,038, or five per cent, one must admit that it is a sound business policy. That is what the average business man is anxious to do-increase his revenue and at the same time decrease his overhead or operating expenditures-and for that reason I say that the national harbours board has made a creditable showing.
Before leaving the port of Montreal I would remind the hon. member for Mount Royal that, if he were sailing to Glasgow, he would have to travel 2.693 miles from Montreal, whereas if he took the ocean limited and sailed from the well known harbour of Halifax, the distance would be 2,407 miles; or making the comparison with Liverpool, from Montreal to Liverpool it would be 2,966 miles, and from Halifax to Liverpool, 2,485 miles. I would call that mileage to the attention of the Minister of Transport. Halifax is the eastern terminal of the Canadian National Railways, and he, as Minister of Transport, should bear in mind that the greater the amount of traffic that goes over the Canadian National railway system, the greater the revenue to that system;
more than that, employees all along the line would benefit.
At the same time I call his attention to the question of the shipment of cattle from Halifax. Last evening we were considering the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, and at that time the question of cattle came up. We have in Halifax sheds which will take care of 1,000 head of cattle, and once again the question of transportation comes into the picture. I suggest to the minister that he bear that in mind and try to divert some of the cattle shipments through the port of Halifax. May I also remind him of the cold storage warehouse with 1,000,000 cubic feet of storage space, completely fitted with freezing, storing and packing equipment and with ample rail connections. I believe the minister is familiar with these features of the port of Halifax. I simply remind him that we have at Halifax all the necessary facilities to handle shipments of cattle and grain from the west as well as package goods for export.
May I refer also to the showing of the port of Halifax in regard to tonnage last year. I regret to learn that Vancouver did not enjoy the prosperity that we did. I am more modest than the hon. member for Mount Royal; I do not say Halifax is the best port in the world, I just say it is one of the best. I was happy to note the increase in revenue last year; not only was there an increase in revenue but there was a drop in the cost of operation. The revenues of the port last year showed a net increase of about 13 per cent over 1936. I was glad the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) mentioned a fish pier. I believe the minister would be well advised to look into the possibilities of the construction of fish piers on both Atlantic and Pacific coasts. It would be an advantage to us in Halifax and to the whole of Nova Scotia if we had not only a fish pier but a public fish market. It would bring fish buyers from the New England states and lead to an increase in the sale and production of fish.

I had some questions to ask the minister on various items as they came up; but when the hon. member for Mount Royal painted such a glowing picture of Montreal, I could not resist drawing his attention to the fact that we have an all year round port on the Atlantic as compared with his six months port in central Canada. With a greater degree of cooperation by the national harbours board, travelling from one part of Canada to another and adjusting matters which may arise from time to time, and cooperation between the harbours board, the province of

I should like to tell the hon. member for Vancouver South why Manitoba grain was not shipped by the Pacific coast last year. It is a shorter haul by way of Fort William, and it is a safer route.

If I may correct the hon.
gentleman, we do not expect Manitoba wheat, but we do expect Peace river wheat, Alberta wheat and part of the Saskatchewan wheat.

There was very little wheat west of Manitoba; that was the reason. A few moments ago I heard an hon. member say, "Vote Liberal and get action." I should like to tell the committee that if there is one department of the government from which we have had action, and honest action, it is the Department of Transport; judging by the spirit of the minister to-night we are going to get plenty of action and it is going to be straight. I should like to say, for the two ports at the head of the lakes, that we feel we are in the safest possible hands; the minister is a business man, an honest man, a brainy man and a good man, and we are proud of him.
The short statement just made by the hon. member for Fort William was interesting, but I was very much surprised that he did not make a stronger plea for the ports of Fort William and Port Arthur.
It is not necessary.

I have been listening to this discussion concerning the different ports and the different rates, the elevation rates, freight rates and ocean rates. I believe this question could be easily solved if the minister would give consideration to the idea-and it will not be long until he will have to give consideration to it-of deepening our waterways and having ocean going vessels go right through to these ports at the head of the
51952-19tJ
lakes. Then we shall get away from this difficulty as between the ports. That is what will come about; we shall have one good port and we shall know who is absorbing all the rates between the prairie farmer and Liverpool. I have been connected with wheat for quite a while, both producing it and handling it in elevators, and I have always found that the farmer absorbs all the rates, elevation, freight, handling, ocean rates and so on, from the day the wheat leaves his farm until it reaches Liverpool. So I was surprised that the hon. member for Fort William did not make a plea of that kind for his ports.

A few hours ago the minister gave a statement of the revenue deficiencies of the various ports in Canada. I was wondering how the port of Albemi showed up in that regard. I think there should be a surplus there, not a deficiency. Has the minister any of the figures for last year at hand?

I am sorry to say that the port of Albemi does not come under this item, and I have not the figures here. There is no possible way to have a deficit at a port which is administered under the Harbours and Piers Act. We go on the principle of no money, no pay; in other words, the expenses can be paid only out of the revenue. The port of Albemi has shown quite a considerable increase in revenue, and I think, when I give the hon. member the financial statement in regard to that port, he will find it very satisfactory.
That may be due to the fact that we have no harbour board there. We have a competent harbour master and a good superintendent, and the result appears to be no trouble, no graft and a profit.

I have listened to everybody talking about ports all over this country. I notice that the port of Montreal had a total of some sixteen million tons, and I was interested to hear the minister say he was partial to that port. Then he. said the port of Vancouver had a total of some 6,-
900,000	tons, and again he said he was interested in and partial to that port. We in Toronto are rather jealous; we had a total of 3,700,000 tons. In fact, Toronto is the third largest port in Canada. We have always had great consideration from the minister, and I know he likes to come to Toronto. We do not trouble him very much; but when we do come to the minister and want something for the port of Toronto, I hope he will always remember-and the house will always remember-that Toronto is the third largest port in Canada, and that the little we do want from time to time we expect to get.
3064	COMMONS
Supply-Transport-Harbours Board

I would not care to create
the impression that I deprecated the growth or development of any port in Canada. I hope the trade and commerce of our country are going to increase to such an extent that every port on the eastern and western borders will receive a satisfactory share of the commerce that is carried on. But I should like the minister to tell the committee the agreed rate for lifting from lake boats into the elevator and from the elevator into ocean boats, at the port of Quebec, that is to be paid by the Dreyfus Company during this current season.

The tariff for the port of
Quebec is exactly the same as for all St. Lawrence ports. The amount that Dreyfus and any other customer of the port of Quebec is paying is S10.25 per 1,000 bushels. It is exactly the same in Montreal, Three Rivers and Sorel.

Then there is absolutely no truth in the statement which appeared in the Montreal press that this company had received a special concession for shipping an agreed amount of grain-that is com, I understand- through the port of Quebec during this season, supposed to be a difference between -SI0.25 and the $1.25 per 1,000 bushels? There is absolutely no truth in the statement that appeared in the press some few weeks ago, leading one to believe that those special arrangements had been made to persuade this company to ship through the port of Quebec this season?

No truth in it whatever.
I ask my hon. friend if he objects to seeing a little movement of grain through Quebec.
Absolutely not.
Why so much talk about it?

I am not talking about it;
I am asking for information.

The hon. member made the
statement earlier that Quebec was getting an undue proportion.

The minister will understand in a few minutes why I ask for this information. He realizes that at the beginning of the season the water rate to Quebec from lake ports was five cents a bushel. This was increased to 51 cents a bushel, and then to six cents a bushel.
What rate is my hon. friend talking about?
On grain.

From where to where?
(Mr. Ross (St. Paul's).]

From lake ports to the
city of Quebec. The rate was increased from five to 51 cents, and then from 5j to six cents. I understand that was as a result of certain arrangements made by the Department of Transport in order that this Dreyfus Company could move grain through the port of Quebec at a special rate which they could not obtain through other ports on the St. Lawrence. The minister has suggested that this is not so, but the fact is that we had this increase in the rate on grain from lake ports to the port of Quebec. I was wondering if there was any significance in the increase made since the season opened.

As a minister of the crown
I told my hon. friend that the rate for Quebec was $10.25, which is exactly the same as the rate for Montreal. Is he prepared to accept that? He seemed to doubt it in his last statement.
I accept it. When an hon. member makes a statement in this house I accept it.

When the rates first came out there was a half cent differential in the rates published for Quebec and Montreal. We took vigorous steps to have that differential removed. We took the position that for many years the river ports of Montreal, Quebec, Sorel and Three Rivers had been quoted uniform rail and water rates. The water rates are not controlled to the same extent as the rail rates, because there is no rate making authority. We took prompt and vigorous action to have the differential removed, and in a short time we succeeded in our efforts. As a matter of fact, no grain moved at the higher rate. The differential was removed as quickly as it had been set up. The rail companies took joint action, but not to the extent of publishing a tariff. They threatened to take action in the same way and put a half cent differential against Quebec, but we threatened to apply to the board of railway commissioners and they changed their minds. We did exactly for the port of Quebec what we are prepared to do for any other port; we did everything to preserve its parity with competing ports.

Had not arrangements been made in the interim to transfer this grain from the Georgian bay ports to the elevators at Quebec by rail at much reduced rates in order to meet that increase by the lake carriers? I am referring to an article that appeared in one of the Montreal papers, I think about two or three weeks ago.

Supply-Transport-Harbours Board

I cannot answer everything that comes out in the Montreal papers. I did not realize they were so unreliable. I can say that we had made no arrangement about rail rates. We did intervene, as I have indicated, to put a stop to the proposed differential in the water and rail rates as between Quebec and Montreal. I believe in taking that step we acted in the best interesits of transportation in this country.
I am sorry that everybody and every source are unreliable except the minister. However, I must take my information where I can get it.
The only difference is that when I make a statement I must be responsible for it.

I try to be responsible for any statement I make. I am seeking information. My curiosity was aroused when I read that report and heard these matters discussed by those who are interested in this particular differential. Let me ask ithe minister one further question. As he knows, in the port of Montreal and at other ports on the St. Lawrence grain is stored free of charge for ten days, after which storage is charged. Is tha/t condition to prevail in the elevators of the city of Quebec, or have arrangements been made to give free storage for longer than the ten days usually allowed?

I feel something like a squirrel in a cage when I answer these questions. I gave an elaborate statement in connection with that situation in which I said that a special tariff had been filed at the beginning of the season to apply until August 31, which provided that during that period there should be no accumulation of storage against full cargoes of export grain at Quebec. We understand that the same practice has been in effect at Sorel and at Three Rivers. The reason for this is that shipment by tramps usually necessitates payment of storage charges which is generally avoided in a port where both liners and tramps are loaded. The position is this. We do accrue that storage at the port of Montreal for periods longer than ten days, but we do not accrue it at Quebec for the period which I have stated. That is provided for in the tariff approved by the board of grain commissioners, and it is available to any one who cares to ship through the port of Quebec.

The minister will appreciate my inquiry in this respect after what was reported in the papers. The people interested in the port placed a great deal of reliance on the statement that was made when the
national harbours board was created. This statement was that the harbours board had stated on innumerable occasions that their intention was to stabilize charges through the different ports and make them uniform. I am glad to have that statement confirmed by the 'minister. I am glad to hear him say that this is the basis upon which the national harbours board are working. I know the people interested in the port of Montreal and in other ports on the St. Lawrence will be glad to have a denial of any rumours and a confirmation of the arrangement that was entered into when the national harbours board was put in charge of the national harbours of the Dominion of Canada. I feel quite certain that, as a result of the discussion to-night, the atmosphere in and around the port of Montreal will be to some extent clarified. I feel all will realize that the Department of Transport is making a serious effort to adjust satisfactorily any differences that might exist and is not attempting to create traffic in one port to the detriment of another. The minister knows as well as I do how these rumours get about and how disquieting they are upon the public. He realizes that if anything is done to create traffic through a particular port by giving special advantages, it will upset the whole scheme and there will be general dissatisfaction and mistrust in connection with the national harbours board. The minister has not given me credit for very much to-night, but I think he will at least give me credit for having supported the bill which set up this national harbours board. At that time I 'made only two suggestions: First, that there should be an advisory committee made up of representatives from the maritimes, the St. Lawrence and the west; or, failing that, that the port managers be given wide authority to work under certain general rules and regulations and not be considered' as merely glorified office boys. These were the only two stipulations I made; and I agree with what the minister is doing. I am glad that the national harbours board is working out so satisfactorily, judging by the statement of the minister, but I hope something will be done so that the cities where the harbours are situated will have more direct contact with the harbours board so that these ports can develop. At the present time there does not seem to be any rivalry between ports, and- the result is that a few ports seem to get the bulk of the business that passes through eastern or western ports. I know the feeling in my own city is that they would like to have more direct contact with the board, and that feeling must be much
3066	COMMONS
Supply-Transport-Harbours Board
stronger in Halifax, Vancouver and Saint John, because Montreal is much closer to the centre of things than these distant ports. I know of cases, however, that come up in Montreal, as the minister well knows, where decisions have to be arrived at almost overnight or otherwise there would be a loss, and I hope that the port managers will be given more latitude or that an advisory committee will be given authority to be consulted in these various areas instead of having everything decided in the city of Ottawa.

I should like to correct one or two misstatements that have been made. One would think, listening to the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), that all the wheat producers of western Canada were in Manitoba, whereas the fact is that Alberta last year produced as much wheat and coarse grains as all the rest of Canada put together.
While we have no seaports in Alberta, we have airports, which are the ports of the future. Listening to the discussion, I came to the conclusion that each member was speaking for his own particular port and considered it the best port in Canada, but the minister realizes that what we really need in the interests of Canada as a whole is the development of our best harbours, wherever they may be, for the shipment of our commodities. Some people talk of the survival of the fittest, and they think the fittest should be considered to be this harbour or that, whereas the survival of the fittest should mean that those ports should survive which give the best service, and I commend to the minister those which are giving the best service to the country.

We have heard considerable criticism about the amount of Canadian grain that is going through United States ports. Can the minister give some idea of the amount of United States grain going through Canadian ports?

There is no uniformity about the thing because it varies with marketing conditions and a number of other factors. For a number of years more United States grain went through Montreal than Canadian grain through New York, and that is likely to be repeated this year. On the other hand, in the winter months the liner demand for wheat for ballast results in a low rate being quoted which attracts some Canadian grain to the port of New York. That has always been and always will be the case. It is dictated by the situation at the moment, and I do not think there is any particular patent on it. But it has been a very unusual
fJ.tr. Walsh.]
year when Canada has not exported far more United States grain than the United States has exported Canadian grain.

Will the minister explain the vote listed under item No. 436, paragraph Ob)? How are these amounts to foe spent? For example, I might mention the item of $130,000 for Saint John and that of $365,000 for Quebec.
The roadway in the rear of berths Nos. 8, 9, 10 and 11, requires an expenditure of $46,000, and frost-proofing shed No. 13 requires $84,000. The roadway is to serve the new berths.
Is the item of $100,000 for " generally unforeseen " available to be spent in any port?
Yes; that is a floating fund to take care of business requirements which develop between times. It is available for any port.
The whole $767,000 will be added to the indebtedness of the national harbours board?
Quite.
What is the total indebtedness to the government and to private individuals?
The total interest bearing indebtedness of all ports to the government is $148,244,183.83.
How much is owing to private individuals as distinguished from the amount owing to the dominion government?
There is, in addition, indebtedness to the public amounting to $23,218,994.76, including the Jacques Cartier bridge.
Is the same rate of interest, which I understood the minister to say is 3i per cent, charged on all indebtedness to the government?
No; the rate of interest has varied depending upon the cost of money at the time the loan was made. Current loans are at 3i per cent, but some are as high as 5 per cent.

Seeing that the indebtedness is all owing to the dominion government, would it not be as well to charge the same rate of interest, 3i per cent, on the whole amount? It seems a little unfair that some ports should be paying more than that.

The loans were made in accordance with the statutes, and the statutes

Supply-Transport-Harbours Board
specify the rate. But we are studying that situation, and it is part of our program to get it adjusted and possibly make changes in the capital structure.
Are the net income deficits added each year to the total indebtedness of the respective ports, and interest charged on the whole amount?
No; we do not capitalize deficits. The deficit is always charged up to the treasury.
And paid out of consolidated revenue?
Yes.

I should like to inquire further about the fire protection problem in Vancouver. The inference to be drawn from the minister's remarks was that the present arrangements there were satisfactory, but as a matter of fact it has been impressed upon me that by reason of recent experience there is considerable apprehension that valuable property may be endangered. There have been several hair-ibreadth escapes from serious conflagrations. Do I understand that the harbours board does not consider it necessary that additional fire protection should be provided? After all, however efficient a city fire department may be, they cannot protect shipping adequately unless facilities are provided for fighting the fire from the waterfront itself.

As I said before, an agreement was made between the mayor and city council of Vancouver and the national harbours board by which there was a division of responsibility. In that agreement, which was a mutual one apparently advantageous to both, the city assumed full responsibility for fire and police protection of harbour property in return for the right of taxation of crown leaseholds.

In view of the statement
made by the hon. member for Royal-I know he would want to be fair-as he gave certain figures, I should like to put on Hansard a statement showing the total quantity of water-borne cargo tonnage landed from and loaded into vessels at the harbour of Halifax during the calendar years 1936 and 1937: 1936, 2,140,458 tons; 1937, 2,376,200 tons; or an increase in 1937 over the year 1936 of 235,742 tons.

I have been an interested and a patient listener to the minister's statements in connection with the cost of moving grain in and out of the harbour of Montreal, and the conclusion I have come to, with which I think the minister will agree, is that it costs just as much to move a given quantity of grain into the harbour and out of the harbour under the new rates as it did under the old. They are just the same.
Exactly the same.

And the argument is
whether it shall be paid in one way or in the other, but the net result is that the cost to some person, whether it be the farmer, the purchaser, or the vendor, is the same.
Exactly the same.

There has been superimposed both upon the harbour of Montreal and over it, the Jacques Cartier bridge. The minister stated that there was an operating surplus. I take it that there is an over-all deficit.
Yes.

What is the amount of
the over-all deficit?

The deficit over-all for the year 1936 was $745,935, and that is after crediting $300,000, paid half by the province and half by the city. The year 1937 is a trifle better; the over-all deficit was $693,479.

The minister says there is an over-all deficit after crediting a contribution made by the city of Montreal and the province of Quebec. That contribution is because of the deficit in the first instance, is it not?

By agreement when the
bridge was built, yes.
But the real deficit, then, is the amount of the two items?
Yes.
The amount of the net deficit plus the amount of the two contributions.
The sum of $993,000 in 1937.
How much?
Practically a million dollars in 1937.
That is what I thought. How does the amount of that deficit compare with the deficit the year before? Is it improving?

Improving a little. Traffic
is better.

Was there any contribution direct or indirect towards the main-

Supply-Transport-Harbours Board
tenance of the bridge that is not included in the operating expenses? Was there some contribution for the relief of unemployment?
Not since 1935, I think. I believe there was some painting done in 1934-35.
By way of contribution?
Yes. Nothing made since.

Mr. 'GREEN: Are any of the supplies for these ports purchased by the harbours board? During the Easter recess I had a complaint about seals for freight cars, of which a great number are used, being purchased in the United States. A seal which was brought into my office had stamped on it "Made in US.A." That may have been just a lone instance, but is there not a policy of the board that all supplies shall be purchased in Canada?
Yes, entirely. I think the harbours board would not buy seals. It must have been-
Freight car seals.
-freight car 6eals, possibly from ex-American lines. But I think the harbours board would not be a purchaser of freight car seals.
New seals used in sealing up freight cars.
If I am not mistaken, they would be supplied by the railroad. In any event, all harbours board material and supplies are purchases of Canadian origin.
Why is item No. 439 separated from item No. 436, and would the minister explain how it comes about that nearly a million dollars of last year's vote was not required?

That arises from a difference in the treatment of public accounts. Certain hafbour assets are carried in the public accounts as active assets, and certain others are carried as inactive assets. The ports of Montreal and Vancouver are carried on the public accounts as active assets because over a period of years they have been able nearly to pay the interest. The other ports are carried as inactive assets because they have not been able to pay more than a small portion of the interest, or none at all.

speechtext:
Is the increase in respect
of pension commissioners the same statutory increase, or is there an additional commissioner?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There is no additional
commissioner; there has been a decrease in the number of commissioners.

Item agreed to.
Direct payments to veterans and dependents -Hospital and other allowances, $1,075,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: What is the explanation of the decrease?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
To some extent a decrease in hospital strength, although I think the hospital strength is about the same. It runs about 2,400 in (the winter, 2,200 in the summer. Possibly the pensioners who in former years went on pay and allowances are either stabilized on pension or do not return to hospital. Our hospital population is becoming more and more veterans' care, and different classes which do not carry pay and allowances. The decrease may be in part due also to the fact that generals, colonels and other officers of high rank no longer receive the pay of their rank, as they did before I came into office.
Mr. GREEN; The reduction on that account would not amount to very much.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Well, seven or eight hundred dollars a month was a lot of money to pay to one man. They are not getting it now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: What is the present position in regard to giving dental treatment? That is becoming a serious matter. It was specifically referred to in the report of the veterans' assistance commission. Apparently a great deal of hardship is suffered by veterans through lack of dental treatment.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
That does not properly come under this item. The question of dental

treatment would come under item No. 223, care of patients, which will not be taken up to-night. But, generally speaking, we give dental care when the disability from which the man is suffering is in some way related to his teeth. We have extended that considerably in the last three or four years. We give all kinds of dental treatment to anyone who happens to be in our hospitals, whatever dental treatment is required. There has been some difficulty, which still exists, with respect to dentures and matters of that kind when the pensioner or patient does not reside in a locality where we have a hospital or a contract hospital or a salaried medical officer of the department. I am endeavouring to place more salaried dental officers in different districts more or less remote from the large centres, so that it will be possible to extend dental treatment to those who require it, even though the dental condition is not directly connected with the disability from which the patient is suffering.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Would it not be possible to have this work done by local dentists? Is it necessary that there be a departmental dentist in each case?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Frankly, it is rather difficult to check up. We do a good deal of it; but the hon. member will realize that there is no treatment which can rim the expense up more, sometimes without much justification, no other treatment which is harder to control than dental treatment; and if we gave it indiscriminately throughout the country, it might get out of control. But we are studying the matter and hope to find a more satisfactory system.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Then we hear complaints about regulations being too strict. For instance, we hear that if a man has a couple of teeith left, he cannot get a plate. The situation may not be as bad as that, but we hear of restrictions that are much too severe. Can the minister tell us what they are?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I shall be glad to give more detail on that vote. I have a statement on the whole dental situation; but I left it with my other documents relating to treatment, because my hon. friend requested that I do not discuss treatment to-night.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There has been considerable alarm among ex-service men with regard to substantial reductions in this item and the item, care of patients. I would appreciate it if either on this vote or the other the minister would give a general picture of the situation. It was reported that for March, 1936, the cost of hospital treatment was $2,760,866; and for

Supply-Pensions and National Health
March, 1937, it was $2,732,087, a decrease of $28,778. For hospital allowances the figure for March, 1936, was $1,315,347, while for March, 1937, it was $1,083,919, a decrease of $231,427. Hospital admissions in March, 1936, were 10,411 and 9,486 for March, 1937, a decrease of 925. The minister will remember that in the proceedings of the special committee in 1936 certain stated questions were submitted to the officers of the department regarding P.C. 91, asking for assurance that there would be no restriction under that order in council as compared with the one previously1 in force. Would the minister, either now or under another vote, tell the committee whether there has been any transfer from class 1 to other classes, thereby reducing the number of men eligible for allowances as class 1 patients?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
My hon. friend will notice that this year the estimates are set out in a different way. In other years the two items, care of patients, and hospital and other allowances, were bulked. The total amount provided in the estimates for these two items was in excess of the actual expenditures incurred for these activities during the past fiscal year. There was an unexpended balance in the vote. I have a comparison here. For 1936-37 the actual expenditures were:
Hospital and other allowances.. $1,083,919
Care of patients	 2,989,446

In the 1938-39 estimates, vote No. 221, which we are now considering, the figures are:
Hospital and other allowances.. $1,075,000
Care of patients, vote 223	 3,045,287

An increase of approximately $50,000 for the two votes put together.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Has the minister the figures of hospital admissions during the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I have that somewhere, under care of patients. But the average is about 2,400. It ran to about 2,580 during last winter and is gradually coming down; I suppose it will reach about 2500 to 2,300 during the summer.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Has there been any substantial transfer from class 1 to other classes under P.C. 91? Are the figures available of those who have been admitted under the various classifications?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: As far as I can get those figures. I shall bring them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
What attention is given to returned soldiers who die suddenly, away from the hospital? I know of a returned
soldier who 'had a job in northern Ontario; he left his place of employment, had to walk some twenty-four miles to the station. About halfway there was a stopping place where he stopped overnight. Next day he started for the station. He had been subject to fainting spells and falling, as the hospital records show; apparently he had one of these spells on the way to the station that day and was frozen to death before he was found. After the post mortem, however, the doctors said he had died as a result of being frozen to death. Personally I do not believe that; the doctors may have been right; but since the man was troubled with fainting spells he might have had one at that time, and not being able to get up again he froze to death. I want to know under what item I should bring this matter up.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I think it might be properly discussed under the item relating to pensions, since I take it my hon. friend proposes to make claim for a pension on behalf of the widow of the ex-soldier who died under those circumstances. As the hon. member knows, the Canadian pension commission has full authority and jurisdiction, without regard to the minister or anyone in this house, to judge whether or not the widow would be entitled to pension.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I have always found them very satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Then I commend my hon. friend to the pension commission, where I have no doubt he will get satisfaction.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: On the question of class 1 allowances I wish to refer to a matter which was referred to previously. Order in council P.C. 91 definitely includes a disability resulting from aggravation while on service. No distinction is made; that principle has been accepted. I think on previous occasions the assurance has been given that there would be no restriction under P.C. 91 as compared with the previous order in council regulating government medical treatment. A number of cases have been brought to my attention recently of men who have been denied class 1 treatment and have not secured the allowances, because the disability resulted from aggravation on service. I shall not take up the time of the committee at the moment to refer to a case cited previously, No. 103431-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is that a Halifax case?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
No; a Seattle case, in which the departmental medical authority definitely stated that since the condition
3072	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health
antedated enlistment, and as it was aggravated only to a very slight degree as a result of service, the man should not be entitled to class 1 treatment. I should like some assurance from the minister that no distinction is made in regard to aggravation cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I think we offered to bring that man back to Canada, but he would not be hospitalized in Canada. Is that the case?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No. If the minister will permit me, the department offered to have this man treated in the outdoor department in Seattle, and the United States veterans' administration replied on January 5 of this year that they had no facilities available for outdoor treatment for such a severe degree of disability. That was dealt with in connection with other matters, but I am asking for some assurance that no discrimination will be made in reference to aggravation cases in regard to pay and allowances, and treatment as a class 1 patient.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am informed, and I have some recollection of it, that the man eventually did get his treatment, did he not?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
He got an increased
pension instead.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I can reiterate my assurance that when P.C. 91 was passed there was no intention to restrict in any way the rights which ex-soldiers had previously enjoyed, and whenever any case like that is brought to my attention I do the best I can to rectify the difficulty.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Is there any
arrangement with the imperial government for giving allowances to imperial ex-soldiers under this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, the imperial ministry of pensions have an office in Canada, at Ottawa, and they make arrangements with their own men. Whatever arrangements are made are as between the ex-imperial soldier and the British ministry of pensions.
Item agreed' to.
Services to veterans and dependents-Employers liability compensation, $40,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
How much of this vote was
spent last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: We expended everything but S2.60.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Has the department given consideration to extending the benefits of this
[Mr. MacNeil.J
compensation? Several recommendations have been made in regard to widening the scope of this regulation.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I do not want to criticize any of my commissions, but when they made those recommendations I do not think they understood what this was about.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The minister should have instructed them better.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I tried to, but still they did not understand. They seemed to think this was a form of group insurance. Frankly, as I have already stated, I do not believe very much good is done ex-service men by means of this $40,000. We pay the claims that are made on account of injuries to ex-soldiers who have been injured in industrial employment. It applies only to those who receive a 25 per cent pension or more. The recommendation, as I understood it, was that this should apply to all ex-soldiers; but under the present set-up of workmen's compensation boards throughout the whole country, as I have already said in the house, the industries are largely insured by industries, and no employer is going to take a new man into his employ simply because he has the assurance that compensation in case of injury will be paid by the government of Canada. The only people who seem to profit by it are the provincial workmen's compensation boards, who are only too glad to make claims on us. We pay the provinces; we have never done anything else. On various occasions I have said I would like to drop this vote; but for some unknown reason there is always a row about it, and it is hardly worth while. We simply give that much money to the provinces. I would say, I think, without fear of contradiction, that in the last ten years not one man has obtained employment on account of this provision.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Would any man lose employment if it was cancelled?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I do not think so. It has been urged that perhaps some of the railways, such as the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian National, might dismiss a man who had more than a 25 per cent disability if his industrial compensation was not covered by this item. That might be so, but I doubt it very much. I do not think the railways would do that.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
